questions.q: What does Row-Level Security control, per this lesson, that ordinary GRANT/REVOKE does not?
options: Which individual rows within a table a role can see or affect, not just whether it can access the table at all
Which columns of a table a role can query
Which tablespace a table's data physically lives in
Which extensions are enabled in the current database
questions.explain: RLS filters access at the row level, inside a table a role already has object-level privileges on, unlike GRANT/REVOKE which operates at the object level.

questions.q: What must be done before a CREATE POLICY takes effect on a table, per this lesson?
options: Row-level security must be enabled on the table with ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY
The table must first be dropped and recreated
The table must be moved to a dedicated tablespace
pg_hba.conf must include a policy line for the table
questions.explain: RLS must first be enabled on the table before any CREATE POLICY definitions take effect.

questions.q: What is the difference between USING and WITH CHECK in a policy, per this lesson?
options: USING filters which existing rows are visible or affected; WITH CHECK validates rows being inserted or updated
USING and WITH CHECK are interchangeable synonyms with identical behavior
USING applies only to DELETE statements, WITH CHECK only to SELECT statements
WITH CHECK disables the policy entirely for SUPERUSER roles
questions.explain: USING governs visibility/filtering of existing rows, while WITH CHECK validates new or modified rows being written under the policy.

questions.q: Do table owners bypass Row-Level Security policies by default, per this lesson?
options: Yes — table owners and superusers bypass RLS by default unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set
No — owners are always subject to every policy with no way to change that
RLS policies apply only to table owners and never to other roles
Ownership has no bearing on RLS behavior at all
questions.explain: Owners and superusers bypass RLS by default, on the theory they already have unrestricted access; FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY changes this behavior.

questions.q: In the tenant_isolation policy example, what does current_setting('app.current_tenant') represent, per this lesson?
options: A session-level variable the application sets after connecting, used to filter rows to the current tenant
A hardcoded value embedded permanently in the table's schema definition
A function that always returns the table owner's name
A pg_hba.conf configuration parameter
questions.explain: current_setting reads a session variable the application sets (e.g., SET app.current_tenant = '42'), which the policy uses to automatically filter rows to that tenant.
